answers.text: Give it a fixed structure - date, item and quantity, then the change, in that order. Keeps the three lines the same each time.
Every claim gets listed the same way - date, amount, category, submitter - then the total's just the sum, so it's the same whoever fills it in.
The dates don't line up - 14th to 19th isn't three days like the email says. Worth checking before it's sent.
The 15% increase in deliveries looks about right.
I'd go with Output 2, it shows the actual numbers behind the 4.1% rather than just the answer.
Reply 2, it's got the order and credit references. Reply 1 doesn't back up its claim.
1. No, that's the customer's own address. 2. Yes. 3. No, not released. 4. Yes, already public. 5. No.
I'd be careful with the pricing terms, and the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies.
I'd check some of the report's numbers against the system before it's sent up.
The order-reading step is the risky one at the start. The gate really needs to sit before the confirmation goes out automatically, checking the extracted quantity against stock.
